1 Purpose

This file is part of a research compendium (Pierce, 2026). It runs a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) on data about dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy at MSU Veterinary Medicine Clinic (VMC) between 2016 and 2022. The study aims to assess the prevalence of bandemia (i.e., band neutrophil elevation) in canine lymphoma patients undergoing CHOP chemotherapy and test predictors of bandemia prevalence. Specifically, we examine the effects of two predictors: the drug administered and the dog’s body surface area (BSA). Some results here are used in a manuscript (Eliason et al., 2026).

3 Methods

Each dog in the sample was undergoing CHOP chemotherapy, which involves administering different drugs according to a multi-phase protocol that stretches over multiple clinic visits. This analysis uses data from visits 1-10 during phase 1 of the protocol. The protocol specifies which drug should be administered at each visit, but there are deviations from the protocol based on clinical circumstances and professional judgement. At each visit, a CBC sample was collected and analyzed to measure the outcome.

We have a multilevel data structure with 530 visits and the associated CBC samples (level 1 [L1] units) nested within 90 dogs (level 2 [L2] units). The number of visits per dog varying from 1 to 10 (mean = 5.9, SD = 3.1).

Due to the high correlation between weight and body surface area (BSA), we have included only BSA in the model.

3.1 Measures

There are no missing data in the measures used in this analysis (see descriptive analysis output file). We centered the predictors to facilitate obtaining unconflated estimates of the effects of variables at each level of analysis (Rights et al., 2020; Rights & Sterba, 2023; Schielzeth, 2010; Yaremych et al., 2023).

3.1.1 Bandemia (Bandemia)

Our outcome for the logistic models is a binary variable measuring whether the CBC sample taken at a given visit exhibited bandemia, which was defined as having total band neutrophils \(\gt\) 0.10 k/ul and coded (0 = No, 1 = Yes). This means that we can interpret estimated marginal means on the response scale as the prevalence rate of bandemia.

3.1.2 Age (Age_Yrs)

Age at the start of CHOP (Age_Yrs) was measured in years. This is a patient-level (L2) measure that was invariant across visits. Prior to modeling, we grand-mean centered this variable to improve interpretation of model coefficients (Schielzeth, 2010), yielding Age_Yrs_C.

3.1.3 Sex (‘Sex’)

Sex is a binary, dummy-coded, patient-level (L2) measure (0 = female, 1 = male).

3.1.4 Body Surface Area (BSA_m2_C)

Body surface area at the start of CHOP (Surface_Area_m2) was measured in square meters (\(m^2\)) at the beginning of the CHOP cycle. This is a patient-level (L2) measure that was invariant across visits. Prior to modeling, we grand-mean centered this variable to improve interpretation of model coefficients (Schielzeth, 2010), yielding BSA_m2_C.

3.1.5 Prior Drug Administered (DrugC_C, DrugD_C, M_DrugC_C, M_DrugD_C)

The drug administered prior to CBC sample collection (Drug) was treated as a nominal, categorical variable with three levels: 1, vincristine (the reference levels); 2, cyclophosphamide; and 3, doxorubicin. This was a visit-level (L1) variable. It was dummy coded into two variables: DrugC codes for whether the drug was cyclophosphamide (0 = no, 1 = yes) and DrugD codes for whether the drug was doxorubicin (0 = no, 1 = yes).

The dummy codes were aggregated to create L2 (patient-specific) means (M_DrugC and M_DrugD). These means were added to the GLMM as L2 predictors so we can properly control for drug when testing the effect of BSA at L2 (Rights et al., 2020; Rights & Sterba, 2023; Yaremych et al., 2023).

While the practice is unfamiliar to many researchers, centering L1 dummy-coded categorical predictors around their group means is necessary for obtaining unconflated estimates of their effects in multilevel models (Yaremych et al., 2023). Accordingly, we computed L1 group-mean centered versions of the L1 predictors, yielding DrugC_C = DrugC - M_DrugC and DrugD_C = DrugD - M_DrugD. The centered variables were used in the models.

3.2 Statistical Analysis

Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a logit link function were employed to assess the effects of each drug and BSA on presence of bandemia. This model was chosen to capture the random effects pertaining to repeated observations from each dog while dealing with the binary outcome. We set the Type I error rate at \(\alpha = 0.05\). We used the glmmTMB package for R to fit the models (Brooks et al., 2017; McGillycuddy et al., 2025).

The basic modeling strategy involved fitting a set of three nested models. We use likelihood ratio tests to compare models in sequence.

  • Model 0 (m0): The null model includes only a fixed intercept and a random intercept. The ICC for this model shows us what proportion of variability in bandemia is attributable to individual differences between dogs rather than to differences between visits for the same dog.
  • Model 1 (m1): This model expands on Model 0 by adding fixed effect slopes for the L1 predictors (centered dummy codes for the drug administered, named DrugC_C for cyclophosphamide and DrugD_C for doxorubicin). It still includes both fixed and random intercepts.
  • Model 2 (m2): This model expands on Model 1 by adding the fixed effect slopes for the L2 predictors. The aggregated means of the L1 drug dummy codes (M_DrugC and M_DrugD) allow us to control for the fact that there was variability in the proportion visits at which each dog was exposed to each drug. We want to control for that when testing the effects of age, BSA, and sex. The model retains L1 effects for the centered drug dummy codes plus the fixed and random intercept terms.
Important

Our manuscript (Eliason et al., 2026) will only report Model 2, but Models 0 and 1 are useful as part of a model building process. They help us better understand the data.

3.2.1 Model Fit Indices

We used the performance package (Lüdecke et al., 2021) to obtain a variety of common model fit indices for GLMMs, including AIC, BIC, ICC, and RMSE. In addition, it also reports the conditional and marginal \(R^2\) (Nakagawa et al., 2017).

3.2.2 Effect Size Estimates

Interpretation was facilitated by using the marginaleffects package (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024) to obtain estimated marginal means for bandemia prevalence associated with each drug along with relevant 95% confidence intervals, risk differences (RD) for bandemia when comparing pairs of drugs, and graphing average predicted bandemia prevalence as a function of each continuous predictor. We also estimated the odds ratio (OR) for each predictor along with 95% confidence intervals.

3.2.3 Collinearity

The performance package (Lüdecke et al., 2021) provides a function for examining the generalized variance inflation factor (GVIF) (Fox & Weisberg, 2019) for terms in regression models. We checked for multicollinearity problems by examining the GVIF and a transformation of it that adjusts for categorical terms that use multiple degrees of freedom (Fox, 2016). In general, one can compare \(GVIF^{(1/(2*df))}\) to cutoffs defined for \(\sqrt{VIF}\). Some suggested cutoffs indicating potential problems are \(\sqrt{VIF} \ge 2\) or \(\sqrt{VIF} \ge 3\). We applied the latter cutoff, so hope to see \(GVIF^{(1/(2*df))} < 3\) in our models.

3.2.4 Model Diagnostics

We used the performance package to do several model diagnostics. First, we used a posterior predictive check comparing model predictions to the observed data. Second, we examined binned residuals by plotting the average residual within a bin against the estimated probability of bandemia. Ideally, all points on that plot should fall within the model’s error bounds.

The DHARMa package in R uses simulation-based methods to compute scaled residuals that should follow a uniform distribution if the data are consistent with the actual distribution used to model the outcome, making it easier to check for deviations from model assumptions (Hartig, 2024). Third, we examined
quantile-quantile plots of those residuals to check uniformity. As usual with a Q-Q plot, data points should lay close to the reference line for the theoretical distribution.

Finally, we examined a Q-Q plot of the random effects to see whether they followed a normal distribution.

We applied all of these diagnostic tests to the models below, summarizing the results in figures.

4 Results

4.1 Model 0 (No Predictors)

Table 2 shows the parameter estimates for Model 0.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0 
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Parameters
#| results: asis

# Null model.
m0 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ 1 + (1 | Patient), 
              data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
              ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)

FN = paste0("Log Likelihood = ", round(logLik(m0), digits = 3),
            ". Deviance = ", round(-2*logLik(m0), digits = 3),
            ". Model df = ", length(m0$fit$par), 
            ". Residual df = ", nobs(m0) - length(m0$fit$par),
            ". 95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 0" = m0), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrrrr", escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "Est.", "CI.LL", "CI.UL", "z", "p"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int", "statistic", "p.value"), 
             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
             notes = FN) %>% 
  cat()
```

Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks. The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. The warning it provides is a result of the low prevalence of bandemia in this sample.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: diag-m0

diagnose(m0)
```
Unusually large Z-statistics (|x|>5):

(Intercept) 
  -9.066624 

Large Z-statistics (estimate/std err) suggest a *possible* failure of
the Wald approximation - often also associated with parameters that are
at or near the edge of their range (e.g. random-effects standard
deviations approaching 0).  (Alternately, they may simply represent
very well-estimated parameters; intercepts of non-centered models may
fall in this category.) While the Wald p-values and standard errors
listed in summary() may be unreliable, profile confidence intervals
(see ?confint.glmmTMB) and likelihood ratio test p-values derived by
comparing models (e.g. ?drop1) are probably still OK.  (Note that the
LRT is conservative when the null value is on the boundary, e.g. a
variance or zero-inflation value of 0 (Self and Liang 1987; Stram and
Lee 1994; Goldman and Whelan 2000); in simple cases these p-values are
approximately twice as large as they should be.)

Figure 1 displays some additional graphs used to check model assumptions. While the binned residuals do indicate minor issues with the model especially for situations where the probability of bandemia is very low or very high, the other panels don’t show any cause for major concern.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: fig-check-m0
#| fig-cap: Diagnostic Checks on Model 0
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 8

check_model(m0, type = "discrete_both", residual_type = "simulated",
            check = c("pp_check", "binned_residuals", "qq", "reqq"),
            base_size = 9)
```

Table 3 shows the intraclass correlation (ICC). This is actually the main reason we ran Model 0. Focus on the adjusted ICC. It shows the proportion of variance in the bandemia that is attributable to individual differences between dogs.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-icc
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Intraclass Correlations

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(26485) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
icc(m0, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(ICC = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Because Model 0 does not use any substantive predictors, we do not expect its fixed effects to explain any variance. Thus, an marginal R2 of 0 is expected. The conditional R2 includes variance explained by both fixed and random effects, so we expect it to be higher than the marginal R2 (usually by an amount equal to the adjusted ICC).

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-r2
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 R2 Measures

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(44512) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
r2(m0, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(R2 = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Another thing to examine is the population marginal mean for bandemia prevalence for a typical dog (random effect of 0), which is shown in Table 5.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-emm-intercept
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for Grand Mean

avg_predictions(m0, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA) %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

4.2 Model 1 (L1 Predictors)

Table 6 shows the parameters for Model 1 and Table 7 shows the corresponding odds-ratios.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1 
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Parameters
#| results: asis

# Add L1 predictors.
m1 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ DrugC_C + DrugD_C + (1 | Patient),
              data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"),
              ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)

# m1 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ Name + (1 | Patient), 
#               data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
#               ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)


FN = paste0("Log Likelihood = ", round(logLik(m1), digits = 3),
            ". Deviance = ", round(-2*logLik(m1), digits = 3),
            ". Model df = ", length(m1$fit$par), 
            ". Residual df = ", nobs(m1) - length(m1$fit$par),
            ". Drug reference level is Vincristine",
            ". 95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 1" = m1), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrrrr", escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "Est.", "CI.LL", "CI.UL", "z", "p"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int", "statistic", "p.value"), 
             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
             notes = FN) %>% 
  cat()
```
Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-OR 
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Odds-Ratios

FN = paste0("95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 1" = m1), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrr", escape = FALSE, exponentiate = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "OR", "OR.LL", "OR.UL"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic,
```

Next, we want to see whether Model 1 fit the data better than Model 0. The resulting LRT in Table 8 shows that accounting for which drug was used prior to the visit improves the model.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m0-m1
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Test Comparing Models 0 vs 1.

#compare_performance(m1, m2)

test_lrt(m0, m1) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors")) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() 
```

Table 9 shows that we still have a similar level of unexplained variability between dogs. That is expected because the visit-level drug predictors were group-mean centered. They can explain variance between visits for the same dog but cannot explain any between-dog variance.

Code 
```{r}

  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(ICC = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

4.3 Model 2 (L1 & L2 Predictors)

Table 13 shows the parameters for Model 2, which includes all the variables we intend to test and Table 14 shows the corresponding odds-ratios.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2 
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Parameters
#| results: asis

# Add L2 predictors
m2 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ DrugC_C + DrugD_C + M_DrugC + M_DrugD + BSA_m2_C + 
              (1 | Patient), 
              data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
              ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)

FN = paste0("Log Likelihood = ", round(logLik(m2), digits = 3),
            ". Deviance = ", round(-2*logLik(m2), digits = 3),
            ". Model df = ", length(m2$fit$par), 
            ". Residual df = ", nobs(m2) - length(m2$fit$par),
            ". Drug reference level is Vincristine",
            ". 95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 2" = m2), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrrrr", escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "Est.", "CI.LL", "CI.UL", "z", "p"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int", "statistic", "p.value"), 
             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
             notes = list(FN, paste("95% CIs reported.")),
             footnote_as_chunk = TRUE) %>% 
  cat()
```
Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-OR 
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Odds-Ratios

FN = paste0("95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 2" = m2), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrr", escape = FALSE, exponentiate = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "OR", "OR.LL", "OR.UL"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int"), 
             gof_map = "none",
             notes = FN) 
```

Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks. The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. diagnose(m2)
```{r}
check_collinearity(m2)
```

Table 15 shows comparisons between Models 0, 1, and 2. It is clear that Model 1 is an improvement over Model 0, and that Model2 is an improvement over model 1.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m0-m1-m2
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Tests Comparing Models 0, 1, and 2.

bind_rows(test_lrt(m0, m2), 
          test_lrt(m1, m2)) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors",
                           Name == "m2" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug)")) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>%

```
Important

We should interpret Model 2 instead of Model 1.

Table 16 shows that we still have had a small decrease in unexplained variability between dogs compared wo what we saw in Model 1. This is expected given that BSA appears to be a meaningful predictor of bandemia in Table 13.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-icc
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Intraclass Correlations

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(74156) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
icc(m2, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(ICC = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Table 17 shows the marginal R2 for Model 2. It is notably larger than it was in Model 1. This is also consistent with the presence of BAS as a meaningful L2 predictor.

Code 
```{r}

set.seed(84361) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
r2(m2, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(R2 = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Table 18 shows that the population marginal mean for bandemia prevalence for a typical dog (random effect of 0) remains similar to that observed in Model 0. That’s what we would expect.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-emm-intercept
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for Grand Mean

avg_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA) %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

Dogs were exposed to different drugs prior to each visit, so one key objective was to examine the bandemia prevalence rates associated with each drug. Table 12 shows the population average estimated marginal means for bandemia prevalence associated with each drug. The estimates assume a typical dog (i.e., one with a random intercept of 0). Figure 4 displays those means.

Code 
```{r}

#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for 
#|          Bandemia by Drug (Main Effect at Level 1)

avg_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                by = c("Name"))  %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(Name, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, 
         s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("Name","EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 3, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2

Fig3 <- plot_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                by = c("Name"), vcov = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = "Drug name", y = "Bandemia") 

Fig3

# Export figure for use in journal submission
ggsave(filename = here(paste0("scripts/output/Figure_3.png")), plot = Fig3, 
       device = "png", width = 4, height = 2, units = "in", dpi = 600)
```
Important

Figure 4 will be Figure 3 in the manuscript we are preparing (Eliason et al., 2026).

The simplest way to compare the bandemia rates is by examining the risk difference between each pair of drugs, as shown in Table 20. The risk difference (RD) is simply subtracting one rate from the other.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-RD-name
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Bandemia Risk Differences Between 
#|          Different Drugs 

# Omit warning message about specifying hypothesis tests using positional 
# indices like b1, b2, etc. I've verified that this is correct. 
options(marginaleffects_safe = FALSE)

avg_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                hypothesis = c("Vincristine - Cyclophosphamide" =  "b1 - b2 = 0",
                               "Vincristine - Doxorubicin" =  "b1 - b3 = 0",
                               "Doxorubicin - Cyclophosphamide" =  "b3 - b2 = 0"), 
                by = "Name")  %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(hypothesis, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, 
         s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("Hypothesis","RD", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 3, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```
Caution

In Table 20 the p-value for the difference in bandemia rates between doxorubicin and cyclophoshamide is not significant but the lower CI bound is just barely below 0. We can’t conclude there is a difference between those bandemia rates even though the point estimate for the risk difference matches that of the risk difference between vincristine and cyclophoshamide. That’s because we have less data about doxorubicin than vincristine, so there is more uncertainty about its marginal mean and differences between it and other those of drugs. You can see that in the wider confidence interval for doxorubicin in Figure 4.

In this study BSA is a patient-level variable rather than visit-level variable because only BSA at the start of CHOP was recorded and used in Model 2. Figure 5 shows the marginal effect of BSA on bandemia prevalence. The prevalence decreases considerably as BSA increases. The predicted value for the smallest dog in the sample is around 19%, while for dogs of average size (centered BSA values of 0) the rate is around 8%, and for the largest dog it is around 2.5%.

Code

```{r}
#| label: fig-m2-BSA

#|          Main Effect at Level 2

Fig2 <- plot_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, 
                         re.form = NA, condition = c("BSA_m2_C"), vcov = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = expression("Mean-centered body surface area (" *  m^2 * ")"),
                     breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5),
                     # Journal wants minus sign ("−") instead of hyphen ("-") 
                     labels = c("−0.5", "0.0", "0.5"),
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . + mean(Final_Patients$Surface_Area_m2), 
                                         name = expression("Uncentered body surface area (" * m^2 * ")"))) +
  geom_rug(aes(x = Surface_Area_m2 - mean(Surface_Area_m2)), 
               data = Final_Patients) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(y = "Bandemia")
```

Table 23 shows comparisons between Models 1, 2, and 3. It is clear that Model 2 is an improvement over Model 1, and that Model 3 is not an improvement over Model 1 or Model 2.

Code 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m1-m2-m3
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Tests Comparing Models 1, 2, and 3.

bind_rows(test_lrt(m1, m2),
          test_lrt(m1, m3), 
          test_lrt(m2, m3)) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors",
                           Name == "m2" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug)",
                           Name == "m3" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug, Age, Sex)"),
         ) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 1 vs Model 2", start_row = 1, end_row = 2) %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 1 vs Model 3", start_row = 3, end_row = 4) %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 2 vs Model 3", start_row = 5, end_row = 6)
```
Important

Table 23 suggests that we should interpret Model 2 instead of Model 3. We can mention in the paper that adding age and sex effects did not improve the model, but that can be a brief aside (just one sentence).

Table 21 shows that in Model 3 neither age nor sex had clear effect on bandemia. Comparing Table 14 and Table 22 shows that adding age and sex to the model makes the confidence interval for the odds-ratio of the BSA effect a bit wider. It widens enough to span a value of 1. The bulk of the CI still suggests the effect is probably negative, but we cannot exclude the possibility of either no effect or a very small positive effect. However, on balance, there remains a fair degree of overlap between the BSA CIs for Model 2 and Model 3 and we have reason to rely more on Model 2.

6 Software Information

This section documents information that is important for reproducibility. Most users will not need to read it. It is primarily here for use by the statistician on the team.

We used R as our main computing environment and Quarto scripts to enhance reproducibility. We used RStudio as the editor to interface with R and Quarto.

  • Software chain: qmd file > RStudio > Quarto > R > knitr > md file > Pandoc > HTML file.
  • Source file: GLMM_Analysis.qmd
  • Output file: GLMM_Analysis_2026-01-29.html
  • Quarto 1.8.27 runs *.qmd files through R and knitr to produce *.md markdown files.
  • Pandoc 3.6.3 converts markdown files (*.md) to other formats, including LaTeX (*.tex) and HTML (*.html) among others.

# Purpose
This file is part of a research compendium [@Pierce-RN8714]. It runs a
generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) on data about dogs receiving CHOP
chemotherapy at MSU Veterinary Medicine Clinic (VMC) between 2016 and 2022. The
study aims to assess the prevalence of bandemia (i.e., band neutrophil
elevation) in canine lymphoma patients undergoing CHOP chemotherapy and test
predictors of bandemia prevalence. Specifically, we examine the effects of two
predictors: the drug administered and the dog's body surface area (BSA). Some
results here are used in a manuscript [@Eliason-RN8603].

# Methods {#sec-Methods}
Each dog in the sample was undergoing CHOP chemotherapy, which involves
administering different drugs according to a multi-phase protocol that stretches
over multiple clinic visits. This analysis uses data from visits 1-10 during
phase 1 of the protocol. The protocol specifies which drug should be
administered at each visit, but there are deviations from the protocol based on
clinical circumstances and professional judgement. At each visit, a CBC sample 
was collected and analyzed to measure the outcome. 

We have a multilevel data structure with `r nrow(Final_Visits)` visits and the 
associated CBC samples (level 1 [L1] units) nested within 
`r nrow(Final_Patients)` dogs (level 2 [L2] units). The number of visits per dog 
varying from `r min(Final_Patients$N_Visits)` to 
`r max(Final_Patients$N_Visits)` (mean = 
`r round(mean(Final_Patients$N_Visits), digits = 1)`, SD = 
`r round(sd(Final_Patients$N_Visits), digits = 1)`). 

Due to the high correlation between weight and body surface area (BSA), we have 
included only BSA in the model. 

## Measures
There are no missing data in the measures used in this analysis (see descriptive
analysis output file). We centered the predictors to facilitate obtaining 
unconflated estimates of the effects of variables at each level of analysis
[@Rights-RN8274; @Rights-RN8755; @Schielzeth-RN1814; @Yaremych-RN8330]. 

### Bandemia (`Bandemia`)
Our outcome for the logistic models is a binary variable measuring whether the 
CBC sample taken at a given visit exhibited bandemia, which was defined as 
having total band neutrophils $\gt$ 0.10 k/ul and coded (0 = No, 1 = Yes). This 
means that we can interpret estimated marginal means on the response scale as 
the prevalence rate of bandemia. 

### Age (`Age_Yrs`)
Age at the start of CHOP (`Age_Yrs`) was measured in years. This is a
patient-level (L2) measure that was invariant across visits. Prior to modeling,
we grand-mean centered this variable to improve interpretation of model
coefficients [@Schielzeth-RN1814], yielding `Age_Yrs_C`.

### Sex ('Sex')
Sex is a binary, dummy-coded, patient-level (L2) measure (0 = female, 1 = male).

### Body Surface Area (`BSA_m2_C`)
Body surface area at the start of CHOP (`Surface_Area_m2`) was measured in 
square meters ($m^2$) at the beginning of the CHOP cycle. This is a
patient-level (L2) measure that was invariant across visits. Prior to modeling,
we grand-mean centered this variable to improve interpretation of model
coefficients [@Schielzeth-RN1814], yielding `BSA_m2_C`.

### Prior Drug Administered (`DrugC_C`, `DrugD_C`, `M_DrugC_C`, `M_DrugD_C`)
The drug administered prior to CBC sample collection (`Drug`) was treated as a 
nominal, categorical variable with three levels: 1, vincristine (the reference 
levels); 2, cyclophosphamide; and 3, doxorubicin. This was a visit-level (L1) 
variable. It was dummy coded into two variables: `DrugC` codes for whether the 
drug was cyclophosphamide (0 = no, 1 = yes) and `DrugD` codes for whether the
drug was doxorubicin (0 = no, 1 = yes). 

The dummy codes were aggregated to create L2 (patient-specific) means (`M_DrugC` 
and `M_DrugD`). These means were added to the GLMM as L2 predictors so we can 
properly control for drug when testing the effect of BSA at L2 
[@Rights-RN8274; @Rights-RN8755; @Yaremych-RN8330]. 

While the practice is unfamiliar to many researchers, centering L1 dummy-coded
categorical predictors around their group means is necessary for obtaining 
unconflated estimates of their effects in multilevel models [@Yaremych-RN8330].
Accordingly, we computed L1 group-mean centered versions of the L1 predictors, 
yielding `DrugC_C = DrugC - M_DrugC` and `DrugD_C = DrugD - M_DrugD`. The 
centered variables were used in the models. 

## Statistical Analysis
Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a logit link function were employed
to assess the effects of each drug and BSA on presence of bandemia. This model
was chosen to capture the random effects pertaining to repeated observations
from each dog while dealing with the binary outcome. We set the Type I error
rate at $\alpha = 0.05$. We used the glmmTMB package for R to fit the models
[@Brooks-RN8667; @McGillycuddy-RN8874].

The basic modeling strategy involved fitting a set of three nested models. We
use likelihood ratio tests to compare models in sequence.

* Model 0 (`m0`): The null model includes only a fixed intercept and a random 
  intercept. The ICC for this model shows us what proportion of variability in 
  bandemia is attributable to individual differences between dogs rather than 
  to differences between visits for the same dog. 
* Model 1 (`m1`): This model expands on Model 0 by adding fixed effect slopes 
  for the L1 predictors (centered dummy codes for the drug administered, named 
  `DrugC_C` for cyclophosphamide and `DrugD_C` for doxorubicin). It still 
  includes both fixed and random intercepts. 
* Model 2 (`m2`): This model expands on Model 1 by adding the fixed effect 
  slopes for the L2 predictors. The aggregated means of the L1 drug dummy codes 
  (`M_DrugC` and `M_DrugD`) allow us to control for the fact that there was 
  variability in the proportion visits at which each dog was exposed to each 
  drug. We want to control for that when testing the effects of age, BSA, and 
  sex. The model retains L1 effects for the centered drug dummy codes plus the 
  fixed and random intercept terms. 

:::{.callout-important}
Our manuscript [@Eliason-RN8603] will only report Model 2, but Models 0 and 1
are useful as part of a model building process. They help us better understand
the data.
:::

### Model Fit Indices
We used the performance package [@Lüdecke-RN8788] to obtain a variety of common 
model fit indices for GLMMs, including AIC, BIC, ICC, and RMSE. In addition, it 
also reports the conditional and marginal $R^2$ [@Nakagawa-RN3697].

### Effect Size Estimates
Interpretation was facilitated by using the `marginaleffects` package
[@Arel-Bundock-RN8812] to obtain estimated marginal means for bandemia
prevalence associated with each drug along with relevant 95% confidence
intervals, risk differences (RD) for bandemia when comparing pairs of drugs, and
graphing average predicted bandemia prevalence as a function of each continuous
predictor. We also estimated the odds ratio (OR) for each predictor along with
95% confidence intervals.

### Collinearity
The `performance` package [@Lüdecke-RN8788] provides a function for examining 
the generalized variance inflation factor (GVIF) [@Fox-RN8789] for terms in 
regression models. We checked for multicollinearity problems by examining the
GVIF and a transformation of it that adjusts for categorical terms that use
multiple degrees of freedom [@Fox-RN3484]. In general, one can compare 
$GVIF^{(1/(2*df))}$ to cutoffs defined for $\sqrt{VIF}$. Some suggested cutoffs 
indicating potential problems are $\sqrt{VIF} \ge 2$ or $\sqrt{VIF} \ge 3$. We 
applied the latter cutoff, so hope to see $GVIF^{(1/(2*df))} < 3$ in our models.

### Model Diagnostics 
We used the `performance` package to do several model diagnostics. First, we 
used a posterior predictive check comparing model predictions to the observed 
data. Second, we examined binned residuals by plotting the average residual 
within a bin against the estimated probability of bandemia. Ideally, all points 
on that plot should fall within the model's error bounds. 

The `DHARMa` package in R uses simulation-based methods to compute scaled
residuals that should follow a uniform distribution if the data are consistent
with the actual distribution used to model the outcome, making it easier to
check for deviations from model assumptions [@Hartig-RN8668]. Third, we examined  
quantile-quantile plots of those residuals to check uniformity. As usual with a 
Q-Q plot, data points should lay close to the reference line for the theoretical 
distribution. 

Finally, we examined a Q-Q plot of the random effects to see whether they 
followed a normal distribution. 

We applied all of these diagnostic tests to the models below, summarizing the
results in figures. 

# Results {#sec-Results}

## Model 0 (No Predictors)
@tbl-m0  shows the parameter estimates for Model 0. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0 
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Parameters
#| results: asis

# Null model.
m0 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ 1 + (1 | Patient), 
              data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
              ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)

FN = paste0("Log Likelihood = ", round(logLik(m0), digits = 3),
            ". Deviance = ", round(-2*logLik(m0), digits = 3),
            ". Model df = ", length(m0$fit$par), 
            ". Residual df = ", nobs(m0) - length(m0$fit$par),
            ". 95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 0" = m0), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrrrr", escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "Est.", "CI.LL", "CI.UL", "z", "p"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int", "statistic", "p.value"), 
             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
             notes = FN) %>% 
  cat()
```

Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks. 
The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. The 
warning it provides is a result of the low prevalence of bandemia in this sample. 

```{r}
#| label: diag-m0

diagnose(m0)
```

@fig-check-m0 displays some additional graphs used to check model assumptions. 
While the binned residuals do indicate minor issues with the model especially 
for situations where the probability of bandemia is very low or very high, the 
other panels don't show any cause for major concern. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-check-m0
#| fig-cap: Diagnostic Checks on Model 0
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 8

check_model(m0, type = "discrete_both", residual_type = "simulated",
            check = c("pp_check", "binned_residuals", "qq", "reqq"),
            base_size = 9)
```

@tbl-m0-icc shows the intraclass correlation (ICC). This is actually the main 
reason we ran Model 0. Focus on the adjusted ICC. It shows the proportion of 
variance in the bandemia that is attributable to individual differences between 
dogs. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-icc
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Intraclass Correlations

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(26485) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
icc(m0, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(ICC = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Because Model 0 does not use any substantive predictors, we do not expect its 
fixed effects to explain any variance. Thus, an marginal R2 of 0 is expected. 
The conditional R2 includes variance explained by both fixed and random effects,
so we expect it to be higher than the marginal R2 (usually by an amount 
equal to the adjusted ICC). 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-r2
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 R2 Measures

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(44512) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
r2(m0, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(R2 = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

Another thing to examine is the population marginal mean for bandemia prevalence 
for a typical dog (random effect of 0), which is shown in @tbl-m0-emm-intercept.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m0-emm-intercept
#| tbl-cap: Model 0 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for Grand Mean

avg_predictions(m0, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA) %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

## Model 1 (L1 Predictors)
@tbl-m1 shows the parameters for Model 1 and @tbl-m1-OR shows the corresponding 
odds-ratios. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1 
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Parameters
#| results: asis

# Add L1 predictors.
m1 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ DrugC_C + DrugD_C + (1 | Patient),
              data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"),
              ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)

# m1 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ Name + (1 | Patient), 
#               data = Final_Visits, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
#               ziformula = ~ 0, dispformula = ~ 1, REML = FALSE)


FN = paste0("Log Likelihood = ", round(logLik(m1), digits = 3),
            ". Deviance = ", round(-2*logLik(m1), digits = 3),
            ". Model df = ", length(m1$fit$par), 
            ". Residual df = ", nobs(m1) - length(m1$fit$par),
            ". Drug reference level is Vincristine",
            ". 95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 1" = m1), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrrrr", escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "Est.", "CI.LL", "CI.UL", "z", "p"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int", "statistic", "p.value"), 
             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
             notes = FN) %>% 
  cat()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-OR 
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Odds-Ratios

FN = paste0("95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 1" = m1), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrr", escape = FALSE, exponentiate = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "OR", "OR.LL", "OR.UL"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int"), 
             gof_map = "none",
             notes = list(FN)) 
```

Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks.
The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. The
warning it provides is a result of the low prevalence of bandemia in this
sample. Because we only added predictors that are dummy codes for drug (a
categorical variable), there is no need to check for multicollinearity.

```{r}
#| label: diag-m1

diagnose(m1)
#check_collinearity(m1)
```

@fig-check-m1 displays some additional graphs used to check model assumptions. 
While the binned residuals do indicate minor issues with the model especially 
for situations where the probability of bandemia is very low or very high, the 
other panels don't show any cause for major concern. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-check-m1
#| fig-cap: Diagnostic Checks on Model 1
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 8

check_model(m1, type = "discrete_both", residual_type = "simulated",
            check = c("pp_check", "binned_residuals", "qq", "reqq"),
            base_size = 9)
```

Next, we want to see whether Model 1 fit the data better than Model 0. The
resulting LRT in @tbl-compare-m0-m1 shows that accounting for which drug was
used prior to the visit improves the model.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m0-m1
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Test Comparing Models 0 vs 1.

#compare_performance(m1, m2)

test_lrt(m0, m1) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors")) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() 
```

@tbl-m1-icc shows that we still have a similar level of unexplained variability 
between dogs. That is expected because the visit-level drug predictors were 
group-mean centered. They can explain variance between visits for the same dog 
but cannot explain any between-dog variance. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-icc
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Intraclass Correlations

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(99487) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
icc(m1, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(ICC = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

@tbl-m1-r2 Shows the R2 measures. The marginal R2 tells us how much of the 
overall variance in bandemia is explained by which drug the dog received prior 
to the visit's CBC sample being taken. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-r2
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 R2 Measures

# Set random number seed to ensure reproducibility of bootstrap result. 
set.seed(32156) 

# Bootstrapped 95% CIs via lme4::bootMer()
r2(m1, ci = 0.95, ci_method = NULL, robust = TRUE, iterations = 100) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  t() %>% 
  data.frame() %>% 
  rename(R2 = X1, LL = X2, UL = X3) %>% 
  head(n = 2) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2)) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

@tbl-m1-emm-intercept shows that the population marginal mean for bandemia 
prevalence for a typical dog (random effect of 0) remains similar to that 
observed in Model 0. That's what we would expect. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-emm-intercept
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for Grand Mean

avg_predictions(m1, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA) %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

@tbl-m1-emm-name shows the population average estimated marginal means for
bandemia prevalence associated with each drug. The estimates assume a typical
dog (i.e., one with a random intercept of 0).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m1-emm-name
#| tbl-cap: Model 1 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) by Drug 
#|          Main Effect at Level 1

avg_predictions(m1, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                by = c("Name"))  %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(Name, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, 
         s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("Name","EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 3, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```



## Model 2 (L1 & L2 Predictors)
@tbl-m2 shows the parameters for Model 2, which includes all the variables 
we intend to test and @tbl-m2-OR shows the corresponding odds-ratios. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2

# Add L2 predictors
m2 <- glmmTMB(Bandemia ~ DrugC_C + DrugD_C + M_DrugC + M_DrugD + BSA_m2_C +

             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic,

             gof_omit = "R2 Marg.|R2 Cond.|ICC",
```


Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks.
The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. The
warning it provides is a result of the low prevalence of bandemia in this
sample. We also check for multicollinearity, but find it is not a problem in
this model.

```{r}

diagnose(m2)
check_collinearity(m2)
```

@fig-check-m2 displays some additional graphs used to check model assumptions. 
While the binned residuals do indicate minor issues with the model especially 
for situations where the probability of bandemia is very low or very high, the 
other panels don't show any cause for major concern. 

```{r}

#| fig-height: 7

            check = c("pp_check", "binned_residuals", "qq", "reqq"),
            base_size = 9)
```

@tbl-compare-m0-m1-m2 shows comparisons between Models 0, 1, and 2. It is clear 
that Model 1 is an improvement over Model 0, and that Model2 is an improvement 
over model 1. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m0-m1-m2
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Tests Comparing Models 0, 1, and 2.

bind_rows(test_lrt(m0, m2), 
          test_lrt(m1, m2)) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors",
                           Name == "m2" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug)")) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 0 vs Model 2", start_row = 1, end_row = 2) %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 1 vs Model 2", start_row = 3, end_row = 4) 
```

:::{.callout-important}
We should interpret Model 2 instead of Model 1. 
:::

@tbl-m2-icc shows that we still have had a small decrease in unexplained 
variability between dogs compared wo what we saw in Model 1. This is expected
given that BSA appears to be a meaningful predictor of bandemia in @tbl-m2.

```{r}

  kable_styling() %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 2, "95% CI" = 2))
```

@tbl-m2-r2 shows the marginal R2 for Model 2. It is notably larger than it was


@tbl-m2-emm-intercept shows that the population marginal mean for bandemia 
prevalence for a typical dog (random effect of 0) remains similar to that 
observed in Model 0. That's what we would expect.

Dogs were exposed to different drugs prior to each visit, so one key objective
was to examine the bandemia prevalence rates associated with each drug.
@tbl-m1-emm-name shows the population average estimated marginal means for
bandemia prevalence associated with each drug. The estimates assume a typical
dog (i.e., one with a random intercept of 0). @fig-m2-emm-name displays those
means.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-emm-name
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Mean (EMM) for 
#|          Bandemia by Drug (Main Effect at Level 1)

avg_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                by = c("Name"))  %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(Name, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, 
         s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("Name","EMM", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 3, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-m2-emm-name
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Estimated Marginal Means (EMMs) for 
#|          Bandemia by Drug (Main Effect at Level 1)
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2

Fig3 <- plot_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                by = c("Name"), vcov = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = "Drug name", y = "Bandemia") 

Fig3

# Export figure for use in journal submission
ggsave(filename = here(paste0("scripts/output/Figure_3.png")), plot = Fig3, 
       device = "png", width = 4, height = 2, units = "in", dpi = 600)
```

::: {.callout-important}
@fig-m2-emm-name will be Figure 3 in the manuscript we are preparing
[@Eliason-RN8603].
:::

The simplest way to compare the bandemia rates is by examining the risk 
difference between each pair of drugs, as shown in @tbl-m2-RD-name. The risk
difference (RD) is simply subtracting one rate from the other. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m2-RD-name
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Bandemia Risk Differences Between 
#|          Different Drugs 

# Omit warning message about specifying hypothesis tests using positional 
# indices like b1, b2, etc. I've verified that this is correct. 
options(marginaleffects_safe = FALSE)

avg_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, re.form = NA, 
                hypothesis = c("Vincristine - Cyclophosphamide" =  "b1 - b2 = 0",
                               "Vincristine - Doxorubicin" =  "b1 - b3 = 0",
                               "Doxorubicin - Cyclophosphamide" =  "b3 - b2 = 0"), 
                by = "Name")  %>% 
  mutate(p.value = display_num(p.value)) %>% 
  select(hypothesis, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value, 
         s.value) %>% 
  kable(digits = 2, format.args = list(nsmall = 2), align = "r",
        col.names = c("Hypothesis","RD", "SE", "LL", "UL", "z", "p", "s")) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>% 
  add_header_above(header = c(" " = 3, "95% CI" = 2, "Wald Test" = 2, " "))
```

:::{.callout-caution}
In @tbl-m2-RD-name the p-value for the difference in bandemia rates between 
doxorubicin and cyclophoshamide is not significant but the lower CI bound is 
just barely below 0. We can't conclude there is a difference between those 
bandemia rates even though the point estimate for the risk difference 
matches that of the risk difference between vincristine and cyclophoshamide. 
That's because we have less data about doxorubicin than vincristine, so there is
more uncertainty about its marginal mean and differences between it and other
those of drugs. You can see that in the wider confidence interval for
doxorubicin in @fig-m2-emm-name. 
:::

In this study BSA is a patient-level variable rather than visit-level variable 
because only BSA at the start of CHOP was recorded and used in Model 2. 
@fig-m2-BSA shows the marginal effect of BSA on bandemia prevalence. The 
prevalence decreases considerably as BSA increases. The predicted value for the
smallest dog in the sample is around 19%, while for dogs of average size
(centered BSA values of 0) the rate is around 8%, and for the largest dog
it is around 2.5%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-m2-BSA
#| tbl-cap: Model 2 Population-Average Predicted Bandemia by Body Surface Area 
#|          Main Effect at Level 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3

Fig2 <- plot_predictions(m2, newdata = Final_Visits, conf_level = 0.95, 
                         re.form = NA, condition = c("BSA_m2_C"), vcov = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = expression("Mean-centered body surface area (" *  m^2 * ")"),
                     breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5),
                     # Journal wants minus sign ("−") instead of hyphen ("-") 
                     labels = c("−0.5", "0.0", "0.5"),
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . + mean(Final_Patients$Surface_Area_m2), 
                                         name = expression("Uncentered body surface area (" * m^2 * ")"))) +
  geom_rug(aes(x = Surface_Area_m2 - mean(Surface_Area_m2)), 
               data = Final_Patients) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(y = "Bandemia")

Fig2

# Export figure for use in journal submission
ggsave(filename = here(paste0("scripts/output/Figure_2.png")), plot = Fig2, 
       device = "png", width = 4, height = 3, units = "in", dpi = 600)
```

::: {.callout-important}
@fig-m2-BSA will be Figure 2 in the manuscript we are preparing 
[@Eliason-RN8603].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-m3-OR 
#| tbl-cap: Model 3 Odds-Ratios

FN = paste0("95% CIs reported.")

modelsummary(list("Model 3" = m3), output = "kableExtra", 
             align = "llrrr", escape = FALSE, exponentiate = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Component", "Term", "OR", "OR.LL", "OR.UL"),
             shape = component + term ~ model + statistic, 
             statistic = c("conf.int"), 
             gof_map = "none",
             notes = FN) 
```

Before we do much to interpret the model, we do some quick diagnostic checks.
The chunk below should return text describing the result of some checks. The
warning it provides is a result of the low prevalence of bandemia in this
sample. We also check for multicollinearity, but find it is not a problem in
this model.

```{r}
#| label: diag-m3

diagnose(m3)
check_collinearity(m3)
```

@fig-check-m3 displays some additional graphs used to check model assumptions. 
While the binned residuals do indicate minor issues with the model especially 
for situations where the probability of bandemia is very low or very high, the 
other panels don't show any cause for major concern. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-check-m3
#| fig-cap: Diagnostic Checks on Model 3
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 8

check_model(m3, type = "discrete_both", residual_type = "simulated",
            check = c("pp_check", "binned_residuals", "qq", "reqq"),
            base_size = 9)
```

@tbl-compare-m1-m2-m3 shows comparisons between Models 1, 2, and 3. It is clear 
that Model 2 is an improvement over Model 1, and that Model 3 is not an 
improvement over Model 1 or Model 2.  

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-m1-m2-m3
#| tbl-cap: Likelihood Ratio Tests Comparing Models 1, 2, and 3.

bind_rows(test_lrt(m1, m2),
          test_lrt(m1, m3), 
          test_lrt(m2, m3)) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(Name == "m0" ~ "No Predictors",
                           Name == "m1" ~ "L1 Predictors",
                           Name == "m2" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug)",
                           Name == "m3" ~ "L1 & L2 Predictors (BSA, Drug, Age, Sex)"),
         ) %>% 
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 1 vs Model 2", start_row = 1, end_row = 2) %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 1 vs Model 3", start_row = 3, end_row = 4) %>% 
  group_rows(., group_label = "Model 2 vs Model 3", start_row = 5, end_row = 6)
```

:::{.callout-important}
@tbl-compare-m1-m2-m3 suggests that we should interpret Model 2 instead of Model
3. We can mention in the paper that adding age and sex effects did not improve
the model, but that can be a brief aside (just one sentence).

@tbl-m3 shows that in Model 3 neither age nor sex had clear effect on bandemia.
Comparing @tbl-m2-OR and @tbl-m3-OR shows that adding age and sex to the model
makes the confidence interval for the odds-ratio of the BSA effect a bit wider.
It widens enough to span a value of 1. The bulk of the CI still suggests
the effect is probably negative, but we cannot exclude the possibility of either
no effect or a very small positive effect. However, on balance, there remains a 
fair degree of overlap between the BSA CIs for Model 2 and Model 3 and we have 
reason to rely more on Model 2. 
:::

# Software Information
This section documents information that is important for reproducibility. Most
users will not need to read it. It is primarily here for use by the statistician
on the team.

We used [R](https://www.r-project.org/) as our main computing environment and
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) scripts to enhance reproducibility. We used
[RStudio](www.rstudio.org) as the editor to interface with R and Quarto.

- Software chain:
  **qmd file > RStudio > Quarto > R > knitr > md file > Pandoc > HTML file**.
- Source file: **`r params$SourceFile`**
- Output file: **`r params$LogFile`**
- [Quarto `r quarto_version()`](https://quarto.org/) runs `*.qmd` files through 
  [R](https://www.r-project.org/) and [knitr](https://yihui.org/knitr/) to 
  produce `*.md` markdown files.
- [Pandoc `r rmarkdown::pandoc_version()`](https://pandoc.org) converts markdown 
  files (`*.md`) to other formats, including LaTeX (`*.tex`) and HTML (`*.html`) 
  among others.
